## Presentation, Awards and Memorials:

**David Michelsen, South Essex Sewerage District (SESD)-A Presentation on Sustaining SESD for the Future**
Board Chairman Mike Parsons introduced Executive Director Dave Michelsen, General Counsel Kristen Kolick, and Mike Collins, Beverly's representative on the District Board.

Mr. Parsons stated that SESD was facing significant financial challenges that could affect its ability to fulfill its statutory mandate. He explained that SESD was seeking an exemption from the limitations of Proposition 2½ and was presenting the issue to its member communities and state legislative delegation. Mr. Parsons explained that SESD's expenses fall into two principal categories: operating costs and capital improvements.

Mr. Parsons explained that SESD operates as a wholesale wastewater provider, receiving wastewater from member communities, treating it and discharging the treated water into Salem Sound. Beverly's local sewer infrastructure remains the responsibility of the city, while SESD assessments are ultimately reflected in local sewer rates.

The District's total annual assessment had remained relatively level at approximately $25 million for many years because increasing operating costs had been offset by declining debt from a major treatment-plant expansion completed in the 1990s.

Mr. Parsons stated that residuals disposal currently costs approximately $4.5 million annually and that the District's favorable long-term contract was expiring. SESD expected FY2028 residuals-disposal costs to increase by approximately $1.5 million to $2 million annually. He stated that this increase could not be absorbed within the existing Proposition 2½ limit.

SESD also faces significant capital needs because much of its treatment-plant equipment is approximately thirty years old and becoming obsolete. One project of particular importance to Beverly is the single wastewater pipeline extending from Water Street to Salem Willows and the treatment plant. Mr. Parsons stated that the line is approaching the end of its useful life and that failure beneath the harbor would present a serious risk.

SESD had retained consultants to prepare a twenty-year capital-improvement plan. The first group of approximately twenty projects totaled roughly $150 million, while the first ten years of planned improvements, including program management, were projected at approximately $390 million.

The Collins Center at UMass Boston analyzed the projected impact on member communities. Beverly's current SESD assessment is approximately $5.3 million. The initial operating increase for Beverly was projected at approximately $390,000, increasing to approximately $760,000 by FY2032. Capital financing could initially add approximately $165,000, with permanent financing eventually adding approximately $2 million to Beverly's assessment.

Mr. Parsons stated that SESD would continue seeking subsidized financing through programs such as the State Revolving Fund, but substantial grants could not be assumed. SESD proposed increasing its Proposition 2½ operating ceiling from approximately $26 million to $30.5 million, which the District projected could provide approximately five to seven years of operating capacity. SESD also sought debt relief for the approximately $390 million ten-year capital program, an increase in its statutory stabilization-fund cap, and modernization of portions of its enabling legislation dating to 1925.

Mr. Parsons noted that other wastewater authorities and municipal enterprise systems are not subject to the same Proposition 2½ limitations. He warned that without relief, SESD could face difficulty developing an adequate FY2028 budget. Potential reductions could affect maintenance at a time when aging infrastructure requires increased attention, potentially resulting in reduced reliability, permit violations, water-quality impacts, fines or regulatory action.

Rotondo asked Budget Analyst Gerry Perry for his initial assessment. Mr. Perry stated that he had only recently received the relevant information and was not yet in a position to independently verify the financial projections or quantify the full impact on Beverly. He stated that he was not surprised by the cost of the infrastructure needs or by SESD's difficulty operating within Proposition 2½.

However, after reviewing draft legislation, Mr. Perry stated that he was not comfortable with the legislation in its current form and believed additional financial guardrails and regulatory oversight should be included to protect ratepayers. Mr. Perry clarified that he was not suggesting SESD had acted improperly. Rather, he believed the size of the financial authority being requested warranted stronger safeguards.

Based on his prior experience with municipal-finance legislation at the Massachusetts Department of Revenue, Mr. Perry recommended that SESD consult with DOR before submitting the legislation. He also suggested considering an independent peer review of the District's capital and financial assumptions.

President Flowers clarified that the Council was not being asked to vote on a resolution or legislative proposal that evening and would have additional opportunities to review the matter.

Houseman commented that, if the legislation authorizing the SESD is as old as he understands it to be, the current financial concerns also present an opportunity to modernize the District's governing legislation and incorporate stronger financial controls and protections for ratepayers.

President Flowers thanked the SESD representatives and stated that the discussion would continue.

**7:30 PM-Order #119-Proposed Amendments to The Beverly Zoning Ordinance: Accessory Dwelling Unit Ordinance.**
President Flowers opened the hearing at 7:30 PM. President Flowers explained that the hearing had originally been intended to be a joint public hearing with the Beverly Planning Board, the agenda had not been posted to reflect a joint hearing. In an abundance of caution under the Open Meeting Law, the City Council would conduct its portion of the public hearing that evening and the Planning Board would conduct a separate hearing.

Planning Director Darlene Wynne introduced Assistant Planning Director Ken Clawson and explained that Beverly had adopted a local Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) ordinance before the Commonwealth subsequently enacted statewide requirements. Portions of the local ordinance therefore needed to be amended to align with state law.

Mr. Clawson explained that Beverly's ordinance, adopted in December 2023, allowed attached and detached ADUs by right in most single-family residential districts, removed family-member restrictions, required owner occupancy, required one off-street parking space and established dimensional requirements.

The subsequent state law requires ADUs by right in zoning districts that allow single-family homes and prohibits certain local restrictions. Mr. Clawson explained that the principal changes include removal of Beverly's owner-occupancy requirement, prohibition of parking requirements for ADUs located within one-half mile of a transit stop, and allowing otherwise compliant ADUs to proceed through the building-permit process without additional zoning relief merely because another portion of the property is nonconforming.

Houseman asked Mr. Clawson to identify the most significant differences between Beverly's existing ordinance and the state requirements. Mr. Clawson reiterated the owner-occupancy and parking requirements and nonconformity changes. He also explained that the state's protected-use standard establishes a maximum ADU size of 900 square feet, while Beverly allows up to 1,000 square feet or one-half the gross floor area of the principal dwelling, whichever is smaller. He confirmed that Beverly's provision is not more restrictive.

**8:00 PM-Order #124-A request for an interdepartmental transfer of $190,000 to support the required shift coverage costs for the Fire Department during FY2026.**
President Flowers opened the hearing at 8:00 PM. Finance Director Bryant Ayles explained that unexpected staffing circumstances resulted in greater overtime use than originally budgeted. The Administration identified six areas elsewhere in the City budget that were underspending and proposed reallocating those already-appropriate funds to the Fire Department. Mr. Ayles emphasized that the request did not involve additional funding beyond what had already been appropriated.

Sonia expressed concern regarding future budgeting rather than the immediate transfer, noting that similar reallocations had been required in prior years. Mr. Ayles explained that the Fire Department had often been able to address overtime overages through internal departmental transfers. FY2026 was tighter, however, and the Department did not have sufficient savings to absorb the full amount. He stated that the overtime line would need to be adjusted upward in FY2027.

Fire Chief Peter O'Connor described FY2026 as an unusual year, with more than twelve firefighters out for extended periods due to injuries, as well as two firefighters who left in August for the Chelsea Fire Department. He explained that the Department normally staffs approximately sixteen personnel per shift but must maintain at least thirteen on duty to appropriately staff apparatuses. When staffing falls below thirteen, overtime must be used. At the minimum staffing level, the Department operates one engine in three areas of the city and one ladder for the entire City. He stated that injuries, employee departures, vacations, and regular leave combined to increase overtime use throughout FY2026.

Houseman asked Budget Analyst Gerry Perry to supplement his written recommendation. Mr. Perry noted that he recommended approval of the transfer and stated that he had confirmed the funds were available. He provided historical context, noting transfers of approximately $58,250 in May 2024, approximately $140,000 several years earlier, and a $235,000 transfer in 2019 from Police Dispatch for fire alarm expenses.

Mr. Perry stated that his principal concern was FY2027. Approximately $810,000 was needed for Fire Department overtime in FY2026, and salary increases under the collective bargaining agreement would also increase future overtime costs. He also noted that approximately $160,000 had been transferred to Dispatch during FY2026, bringing transfers into Public Safety during the fiscal year to approximately $350,000. (v) the dealer's unfair and deceptive acts or practices, misrepresentations, failure to disclose material facts or failure to honor a warranty or arbitration order in a retail transaction; or
(vi) the dealer's failure to pay off a lien on a vehicle when the dealer had assumed the obligation to pay off the lien in the sale of the vehicle.

(2) Recovery against the bond or its equivalent may be made by any person who obtains a final judgment in a court of competent jurisdiction against the dealer for an act or omission against the bond on which the bond is conditioned if the act or omission occurred during the term of the bond. Every bond shall also provide that no suit may be brought to enforce any liability on the bond unless brought within 1 year after the event giving rise to the cause of action.

(3) A separate bond or its equivalent shall cover only those acts and omissions described in clauses (i) to (vi), inclusive, of paragraph (1). The surety on a bond shall not be liable for total claims in excess of the bond amount, regardless of the number of claims made against the dealer during the term of the bond.

(4) In lieu of the bond required by this section, the municipal licensing authority may allow the dealer to deposit collateral in the form of a certificate of deposit or irrevocable letter of credit, authorized by any banking laws of the commonwealth, which has a face value equal to the amount of the bond otherwise required. The collateral may be deposited with or substituted for, by the commonwealth, interest on the certificate of deposit shall be payable to the dealer who has deposited it as collateral, or to a person at the dealer or the bonding authority direct.

(5) A surety shall provide to the municipal licensing authority notice of cancellation of the bond within 30 days of the cancellation. Upon receipt of notification from a surety that a bond has been cancelled, the municipal licensing authority shall notify the licensee that he has 10 days to comply with the bond requirement. If the licensee does not comply with this 10 day period, the municipal licensing authority shall revoke the Class 2 license and shall notify the licensee who shall surrender any dealer plate issued to the licensee pursuant to section 5 of chapter 90.

(6) A municipal licensing authority shall not issue or renew a Class 2 license unless it is satisfied that a bond or equivalent proof of financial responsibility meeting the requirements of this section is in effect during the term for which the license shall be issued or renewed, and that the dealer maintains or demonstrates access to repair facilities sufficient to enable him to satisfy the warranty repair obligations imposed by said section 7N1/4 of chapter 90. A used car dealer shall remain liable for all warranty repairs and other obligations imposed by said chapter 90.

(d) Class 3. A dealer whose principal business is the buying of second hand motor vehicles or parts thereof for the purpose of resale of parts of second hand motor vehicles may be granted a motor vehicle junk license. The registrar shall adopt rules and regulations defining sufficient repair facilities for the purposes of subsection (b) and paragraph (4) of subsection (c).

### Section 59. Licensing authorities; expiration; fees; application; prerequisites; premises; ordinance regulations; revocation.
The police commissioner in Boston and the licensing authorities in other cities and towns may grant licenses under this section which shall expire on January first following the date of issue unless sooner revoked. The fee for the license shall be fixed by the licensing board or officer, but in no event shall any such fee be greater than $200. In each such case such license shall be revoked, the licensing board or officer shall forthwith notify the registrar of such revocation. Any person aggrieved by any action of the licensing board or officer refusing to grant, or revoking a license for any cause may, within ten days after such action, appeal to any justice of the superior court in the county in which the premises sought to be occupied under the license or permit applied for are located. ## Environmental Cleanup Update

150 Sohier Road Property, Beverly MA | FALL 2026

*This annual fact sheet provides an overview of the status of environmental investigation and treatment of the former Varian Facility at 150 Sohier Road in Beverly, Massachusetts.*

### Varian Completes System Installation and Continues Environmental Treatment

Throughout 2026, the Varian project team continued to implement the environmental cleanup plan. This work has included continuing to operate existing treatment systems and beginning operation of new treatment systems for indoor air, soil, shallow groundwater, and bedrock groundwater at the former Varian Site.

The Site environmental remedies include five treatment areas (Figure 1):

- PSL-10 (Open Field) Source Area
- Bedrock near Buildings 3 and 5
- Building 3 Source Area
- Stream A Seep
- Building 5 Source Area

In 2026, two new treatment systems started operation – injection treatment below Building 5 (spring 2026) and the thermal system below Building 3 (summer 2026).

A Temporary Solution Statement was submitted for the former Varian Site in February 2024 to the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP). This statement, prepared by a Massachusetts Licensed Site Professional (LSP), demonstrated that the Site does not pose a human health risk, but that treatment needs to continue to achieve a Permanent Solution. Sampling results from the Site continue to support this conclusion. The remedies being implemented are expected to accomplish the additional treatment needed for a Permanent Solution.

Public updates occur during the year through Public Involvement Plan and Technical Advisory Group meetings. In addition, the Varian project team submits Phase IV Status Reports twice a year in accordance with MassDEP requirements, as well as monthly updates distributed to the public mailing list and posted on the project website (https://beverlysitecleanup.com/). ### Site History and Overview

The former Varian Facility, located at 150 Sohier Road, is currently owned by another firm and operates as an active manufacturing facility for microwave and radar products. The 150 Sohier Road property has been used as an industrial facility since the early 1950s. Industrial solvents were released to the environment due to the chemical handling and disposal practices that were common at the time, before stricter environmental regulations were enacted. These solvents, used primarily for surface treatment, cleaning, and degreasing operations, included trichloroethene (TCE), perchloroethene (PCE), and 1,1,1-trichloroethane (TCA). Releases of these solvents occurred in three main areas: the Building 3 area, the Building 5 area, and an open field known as potential source location (PSL) 10. TCE, PCE, and TCA are heavier than water and have limited ability to dissolve in water. They also tend to evaporate easily and are referred to as volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Varian, with support from Jacobs Solutions, has investigated and is actively cleaning up the Site in accordance with Massachusetts regulations, known as the Massachusetts Contingency Plan (MCP). The Site is listed by MassDEP as Site Number 3-0485.
